..

Through next Wednesday...

Dry westerly flow will continue to bring very warm/dry weather 
today and Friday. Look for highs in the mid 70s east to lower 80s 
west today. Downslope winds/warming become enhanced on Friday 
ahead of an approaching trof. This will push temps well into the 
80s and some central/eastern locations may push 90F with 700mb 
temps to +10c and deep mixing. Is this really over a week into 
October? Main concern Friday is fire weather due to the heat, 
breezy winds (gusts 35-45 mph along western foothills) and low RHs
(near 10%). A Fire Weather Watch remains in effect from noon to 
9pm for western and southern foothills...areas that did not 
receive significant rainfall in September. Please be careful not 
to spark a fire!

Cold front arrives early Saturday bringing a shift to brisk N-NE 
winds and falling temperatures. One thing to monitor is potential 
for modest mountain waves in the lee of the Beartooths and 
Bighorns in the few hours prior to the fropa. Could see ~40 mph 
gusts (and fluctuating temps) at places like Red Lodge, Fort Smith
& Dayton late Friday night. Behind the frontal passage, as a trof
continues to deepen over the PacNW (w/ origins in NW Canada), the
risk of showers will increase in the west on Saturday. In fact, 
snow will begin over the Crazy & Beartooth Absaroka Mountains, and
snow levels may fall enough to get a change to wet snow at places
like Judith Gap & Melville by late afternoon. A BIG change over a
24-hr period.

The combination of large scale ascent from a deep low over the 
western great basin, deepening E-SE upslope winds in our region
and much colder temperatures brings the first risk of lower 
elevation snow of the fall. This is confidently the coolest air 
mass yet of the fall and widespread precipitation is a near 
certainty from Saturday night to Monday. Lack of confidence 
continues for ptype and potential snow accumulations, which will 
no doubt have a great deal of elevation dependency when all is 
said and done. The warm ground from a very warm start to October
will also play a role. It does look like a changeover to wet snow
for most west/central parts by daybreak Sunday, and any 
accumulation by then will help to hold temps down on Sunday. 
Looking at probabilities, the chance of 1" of snow is 10-20% over 
the east, 50% central areas (including Billings) and 80-90% along 
western foothills. The chance of 6" of snow is 15% from Roundup to
Billings & Sheridan, and 45-55% along the western foothills. 
Ensembles continue to show plenty of spread in what will remain a 
complicated forecast. Western mountains will see heavy snowfall (a
50-70% chance of 12" or more).

A couple other items to note. Models still show a weaker split
trof over western MT Monday, keeping ascent and the risk of
rain/snow going before the main upper low over the SW CONUS
becomes completely cut off. Also, moisture from remnants of
Hurricane Rachel (currently west of Baja) is expected to lift thru
the SW flow and brush southeast MT Sunday night into Monday. 
Ensembles show pwats near 200% of normal in far southeast MT 
during this time. If lee side air mass is sufficiently cold for 
snow, there could be heavy snow to deal with over southeast MT, 
especially over the higher hills which would include heavily 
traveled divides (e.g. Home Creek & Lame Deer). Today's forecast 
reflects increased precip potential over our east Sunday night & 
Monday. Again, a lot of small scale uncertainty to be worked 
through yet.

Potential impacts with this wintry system include travel, weighing
down of leafy tree limbs (cannot rule out tree damage and power 
outages), and outdoor recreation. There is also a good chance of 
the first freeze of the season for most of the region by Monday 
night.

There remains uncertainty when exactly the precip tapers off...the
consensus seems to be Monday but light precip could linger into 
Monday night. After highs in the 30s & 40s Sunday & Monday, 
Tuesday is looking dry & warmer with highs into the 50s. By 
Wednesday, there may or may not be an additional shortwave from 
the NW, which could attempt to eventually phase with the SW cut 
off low. Large uncertainty in how these pieces evolve, but overall
the weather pattern looks to remain active and on the cool side 
through the middle of next week.

JKL
